title: "The practical work"

This page is your **roadmap** for the hands-on sessions. It tells you *what* to do and *why*, not *how*: you write your own code, in your own notebook, with the tools presented in the lectures (`spatialdata`, `scanpy`, `squidpy`). Their documentation is part of the course material: read it, try things, look at what the objects contain.

## How we work

- **One notebook per person**, saved in your personal folder (`trainees/<your folder>`, see [Before the course](index.qmd#before)).
- **Every step has a goal and a few questions.** Write your choices and your answers in text cells next to the code (why this threshold, what you see in this plot): they matter more than the code.
- **Your choices first, the paper afterwards.** Choose your filters and parameters yourself and justify them with plots. Then compare with what the authors did: keep the paper at hand, in particular the STAR Methods (*ST-seq data processing*).
- **Talk to each other.** Compare thresholds, plots and interpretations with your neighbours: two different choices, both justified, are often the most interesting part of the discussion.
- **Ask us, Sergio and Marco**, at any time: about the biology, the methods, or a technical problem. Do not stay stuck on an error for more than 10 minutes.
- **At the end of the course** we will share our own notebook, run on the same data, so that you can compare it with yours.

## Getting started

In JupyterLab, go to your folder (`ifbdata` → `spatial_cell_id` → `CNRS_Formation_Entreprise` → `trainees` → your folder) and create a new notebook with the **Python cnrs-st** kernel. In its first cell, after the imports, define where the data are and where your results go:

```python
BASE = "/home/jovyan/ifbdata/spatial_cell_id/CNRS_Formation_Entreprise"
DATA = f"{BASE}/DATA_CNRS"          # the data: read only
OUT = f"{BASE}/trainees/mrossi"     # your folder: replace mrossi with yours
```

**The data** (in `DATA_CNRS`):

```
DATA_CNRS/
├── visium/
│   ├── Donor1_Skin/        one folder per section (16): count matrix,
│   ├── ...                 H&E images and spot positions
│   ├── Donor4_Wound30/
│   └── GSE241124_spatialseq_metadata_acutewound.txt   authors' spot annotation
├── paper_marker_genes.csv  marker genes reported in the paper
└── sc_reference_mod.h5ad   scRNA-seq reference, for Day 2
```

- **16 sections** = 4 donors × 4 conditions: healthy skin (`Skin`), and the wound 1, 7 and 30 days after injury (`Wound1`, `Wound7`, `Wound30`).
- **Sequencing batches:** Donor3 and Donor4 were sequenced together, Donor1 and Donor2 separately. So there are 4 donors but only 3 batches: donor and batch are not the same thing.
- **Donor3 and Donor4** are also in the scRNA-seq dataset of the same study: this is what makes the sc–st integration of Day 2 meaningful.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Save checkpoints
At the end of each part (after filtering, after clustering, at the end of your project), write your `SpatialData` object to a `.zarr` file in `OUT`. If the kernel dies, if you come back the next day, or if you start a new VM, you restart from there instead of from the beginning.
:::

## Day 1 · Fundamentals {#day1}

### Step 1 · Discover the data (13:30, about 20 min)

**Goal:** understand what a Visium section looks like in Python, then put the 16 sections together.

- Open **one section** (for instance `Donor4_Wound7`) as a `SpatialData` object and print it. What are the *images*, the *shapes*, the *tables* and the *coordinate systems*? Where are the counts, and where are the positions of the spots?
- Plot the H&E image with the spots on top.
- Load the **16 sections** into one object. Add to the table the information you will need later: sample, donor, condition, sequencing batch, and the authors' annotation from their metadata file (it only exists for the spots they kept).
- Look at the 16 H&E images side by side.

**To discuss:** how different are the sections (size, shape, pieces of tissue)? Can you see the wound on the H&E alone?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Technical trap: spot names when merging the sections
The spot barcodes are the same in every section (same slide design). If you merge the sections as they are, the names are made unique by adding `-1`, `-2`... and no longer match the authors' metadata. Add the sample name in front of the barcodes **before** merging: the names become `Donor1_Skin_AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1`, exactly the format of the metadata.
:::

### Step 2 · Quality control and filtering (about 14:00–15:00)

**Goal:** decide which spots and which genes to keep, and be able to justify it.

- Compute the usual QC metrics per spot (counts, detected genes, mitochondrial and haemoglobin fractions) and look at which genes take most of the counts.
- Compare the sections: medians and distributions.
- **Plot the QC metrics on the tissue**, one donor at a time (its 4 sections side by side).
- Choose your filters for spots and genes. Before deciding, check how much of *each section* a threshold would remove. Write down your choice and why.
- **Only then**, compare with the authors: their metadata contain only the spots they kept. How many spots did you remove, and how many did they? Where do the two choices differ, on the tissue and in the QC metrics? What could explain the difference?
- Save a checkpoint.

**To discuss:**

- A spot is not a cell. What can a spot with few genes be, on the tissue?
- In single-cell data, a high mitochondrial fraction flags damaged cells. Is it the same in an intact tissue section? Would a typical single-cell filter remove a whole tissue compartment here?
- The sections have very different depths. Does the same threshold make sense for all of them?
- Some very abundant genes say little about the tissue. Which ones, and should they stay in the matrix?

### Step 3 · Normalisation, dimensionality reduction, clustering (15:00)

**Goal:** a first picture of the expression structure across the 16 sections.

- Keep a copy of the raw counts: you will need them for differential expression and on Day 2.
- Normalise, select highly variable genes, run a PCA. Colour it by donor, condition and depth.
- Build the neighbour graph, the UMAP, and cluster (Leiden). Colour the UMAP by donor, sequencing batch, condition and cluster, and count how the spots of each cluster are distributed across donors, batches and conditions.
- Is there a cluster made of low-depth spots only?

**To discuss:**

- What drives the main axes of variation: biology (condition), donor, batch, depth?
- Are the clusters shared across sections, or specific to one donor or one batch? Is that technical or biological? Do **not** correct anything today: integration is for Day 2.
- In space, the total count of a spot also depends on how many cells it contains. Is library-size normalisation completely neutral here?

### Step 4 · Marker genes and annotation

**Goal:** give a name to each cluster.

- Find the marker genes of each cluster.
- Look at the marker genes reported in the paper for the ST clusters (`paper_marker_genes.csv`).
- Give each cluster a name.

**To discuss:** a 55 µm spot contains several cells. Are you naming cell types, or tissue regions?

### Step 5 · Back to the tissue

**Goal:** check on the image what the clusters and the genes mean.

- Plot the clusters on the H&E, one donor at a time.
- Plot a few genes on the 4 sections of a donor, **with the same colour scale for all the panels** (otherwise each panel is stretched to its own range and the time points cannot be compared). Genes of activated keratinocytes are a good way to find the wound edge.
- Save a checkpoint.

**To discuss:** are the clusters continuous regions on the tissue, or scattered spots? Where is the wound in each section?

### If you have time (otherwise on Day 2)

- **Spatially variable genes.** One section at a time, build the spatial graph of the spots and rank genes by spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I). How is a *spatially* variable gene different from a *highly* variable gene? Which structures do the top genes describe?
- **Differential expression between conditions** (for instance Wound7 against Skin). The statistical unit is the **donor**, not the spot: sum the counts per section (pseudobulk) and use a paired design (donor + condition). Why would a test between thousands of spots give misleading p-values?

**16:30 · Wrap-up.** Your QC choices and their consequences, the donor and section effects you saw, what you would do tomorrow.

## Day 2 · Your project {#day2}

### Step 6 · Choose a question (end of the morning lecture)

In small groups, choose one option:

| Option | Sections | Question |
|---|---|---|
| **A** · Time course in one person | Donor4: Skin, Wound1, Wound7, Wound30 | How do the regions of the wound change over time? Which cell types are where? |
| **B** · Reproducibility across people | Wound7 of the 4 donors | Are the wound regions the same in every donor? What is batch, what is biology? |
| **C** · Everything | the 16 sections | Regions shared by the whole cohort, and how they change over time in each donor |

In every option the path is the same: integration across sections → spatial domains → description of the domains → cell types in space → one biological message, with its limits.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Ready-made code: keep only the sections of your option
This is `SpatialData` plumbing, so here it is. A section is made of its spots (named like the section) and of two images; the table is filtered with them. Keep the line of your option and comment the others.

```python
sdata = sd.read_zarr(f"{OUT}/visium_clustered.zarr")     # your checkpoint of Day 1

GROUP_SAMPLES = ["Donor4_Skin", "Donor4_Wound1", "Donor4_Wound7", "Donor4_Wound30"]        # option A
# GROUP_SAMPLES = ["Donor1_Wound7", "Donor2_Wound7", "Donor3_Wound7", "Donor4_Wound7"]     # option B
# GROUP_SAMPLES = SAMPLES                                                                   # option C

hires = [f"{s}_hires_image" for s in GROUP_SAMPLES]
lowres = [f"{s}_lowres_image" for s in GROUP_SAMPLES]
elements = GROUP_SAMPLES + hires + lowres
sdata_g = sdata.subset(elements, filter_tables=True)
adata_g = sdata_g["table"]
adata_g.obs["sample"] = adata_g.obs["sample"].astype("category").cat.remove_unused_categories()
```
:::

### Step 7 · Integration across sections (10:30)

**Goal:** remove the differences between sections that are not biology, without removing the biology.

- Recompute the highly variable genes and the PCA on your sections.
- Correct the section effect (for instance with Harmony on the PCA; another method is fine if you can justify it). One method, well checked, is enough: do not spend the morning comparing methods.
- Check the result: compare the clusters before and after, section by section.

**To discuss:** in your option, what is a section: a batch, a donor, a time point? Could the correction erase real differences (think of option A)? Which structures should mix across sections, and which should stay separate?

### Step 8 · Spatial domains

**Goal:** find regions of the tissue, using the position of the spots and not only their expression.

- Expression clusters ignore where the spots are, so on the tissue they often look like "salt and pepper". Spatially aware methods also use the neighbours of each spot. We use **CellCharter**: it adds to each spot the average profile of its neighbours, ring after ring on the spatial graph, then clusters this representation.
- Plot the domains next to the expression clusters, on the tissue.
- Change one parameter at a time (number of rings of neighbours, clustering resolution, with or without integration) and look at the effect.

**To discuss:** are the domains continuous on the tissue? Which ones appear only in the wounds? What would be a "ground truth" for spatial domains?

### Step 9 · Describe the domains

**Goal:** turn the domains into tissue regions with a name.

- Find the marker genes of each domain and name it.
- Look at the composition of each section: which fraction of its spots falls in each domain? How does it change over time (option A) or between donors (option B)?
- Neighbourhood enrichment: which domains border which?

**To discuss:** the diagonal of the neighbourhood matrix is always strong (domains are continuous by construction). What does the rest of the matrix tell you?

### Step 10 · Cell types in space: sc–st integration (13:30)

**Goal:** find where the cell types identified by scRNA-seq are located in the tissue.

- The reference `sc_reference_mod.h5ad` contains raw counts of scRNA-seq cells from Donor4 and Donor3 (all time points), with the authors' cell types in the column `cell_type`. Keep the raw counts before normalising it.
- **Approach 1 · signature scores:** find marker genes of each cell type in the reference, then score the spots with them.
- **Approach 2 · Tangram** (`clusters` mode), one section at a time: it learns where to place the profile of each cell type so that the predicted expression matches the measured one.
- **Check:** do the two approaches agree? Do they agree with single marker genes measured directly in the spots (an independent check)?
- Plot a few cell types on the tissue.

**To discuss:**

- In `clusters` mode, what does a Tangram value say: *where* a cell type is, or *how many* cells there are?
- Can rare cell types be trusted with 55 µm spots?
- In option B, the reference comes partly from other people: how far can a reference be "borrowed"?
- Cell2location, often used in papers, is much more accurate for proportions, but needs hours on a CPU: this is why we do not use it here.

### Step 11 · Domains and cell types, over time

**Goal:** connect everything into one message.

- In which domains does each cell type go? Which cell types make up each domain?
- Combine this with the composition of the sections over time (option A) or across donors (option B).
- Optional, if you want statistics: differential expression *within one domain* between conditions (pseudobulk, as on Day 1). With one donor (option A) there are no replicates: only descriptive statements are possible.
- Save a checkpoint.

### Step 12 · Presentation (15:30, about 10 minutes per group)

A few slides, with:

- the question, the sections you chose, and why;
- your QC and filtering decisions, in one slide;
- the integration: before and after, and how you checked that it did not erase biology;
- the spatial domains on the tissue, with their marker genes and a name;
- the cell types in space, with one independent check;
- **one biological message** (for instance: "the wound-edge domain appears at Wound1, is largest at Wound7 and is rich in myeloid cells"), and its **limits**: spot resolution, number of donors, borrowed reference, differences in depth between sections.

## When something goes wrong

- Read the **last line** of the error message first.
- `FileNotFoundError`: check `DATA` and `OUT`, character by character.
- `ModuleNotFoundError`: the notebook is not using the **Python cnrs-st** kernel.
- `KeyError` on a gene: the gene was removed by your filters, or does not exist under that name.
- Error when writing a `SpatialData` object about invalid names: column names with spaces or `&` are refused; rename them.
- Still stuck after a few minutes: ask Sergio or Marco.
